title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hookLine: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
carry: the guest is god: light the way

cards: You've heard Diwali's great story: Rama coming home to Ayodhya after fourteen years in the forest, and a city lighting lamps to show him the way. Tonight, look at the lamps themselves.
It's the new-moon night of the month of Kartika, in autumn. No moon at all. On every windowsill, every doorstep, every railing, there's a small clay dish of oil with a cotton wick.
Dozens of them. Hundreds, on a single street. Somebody's grandmother has been on her knees since the afternoon, drawing a pattern in colored powder at the front door.
The door is wide open. Somebody is expected.

teach.h: DEEPA, A LAMP. AVALI, A ROW.
teach.b: Diwali is the everyday form of the Sanskrit Deepavali. Deepa is a lamp. Avali is a row.
A row of lamps: the whole festival in two words. Not one big light, but a row of small ones, each a clay dish you could hold in your palm.
And they come on the darkest night on purpose, the new moon of Kartika. If you wanted to show light winning, you'd pick exactly this night. So who is expected?
Rama, in the Ramayana's story. And in many homes, on the main night, Lakshmi too, the Goddess of wealth and good fortune.

teach.h: A CLEAN HOUSE, AN OPEN DOOR.
teach.b: Families clean the house from top to bottom in the days before, because the tradition says she comes to homes that are clean, bright and open. They draw rangoli, those patterns of colored powder, at the threshold.
They leave doors and windows open and lamps burning so she can find the house. The whole night is an act of welcome: a clean house, a lit path, an open door.
Hindus grow up with an old Sanskrit line for this: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you. On Diwali it runs both ways.
God is welcomed like a guest, and every guest who walks in is welcomed like God. And look at who the lamps are for. You can see your own house without them.
They're for someone coming in out of the dark. The guest is God.

how: At Diwali, Hindus clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps on the new-moon night of Kartika, worship Lakshmi, open new account books, share sweets and visit family.

games.q: it's the new-moon night. you have oil, wicks and a pile of small clay dishes. how do you light the house?
o: one big lamp in the middle of the room.
a row of small lamps along every sill and step.
no lamps until the moon comes up.
games.why: the festival's name is the answer: deepa, a lamp; avali, a row. many small lights, set out for someone coming home in the dark.

practice: If you can, light a candle, or switch on one small lamp and turn the others off; if you can't, picture a clay lamp on your windowsill, and watch the flame.

Think of the people who come home to you, or the ones you come home to: a partner on a late shift, a kid walking back from school, a parent you visit on Sundays. Picture your small light at the door, already lit, when they arrive.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. From Deepavali, a row of lamps, lit on the darkest night of Kartika for someone coming home.

orig.note: Sanskrit: deepa, a lamp, and avali, a row. Diwali is its everyday form.
